---
title: "Farrington"
---

Farrington asks the same question as RKI: is this week high *for this time of
year*? RKI averages comparable weeks from past years. Farrington fits a
regression line through them instead, so the expected count can follow a trend,
and the scatter of ordinary weeks is measured, not assumed. It was built in
England and Wales to screen weekly laboratory reports [@farrington1996], and
@salmon2016 call it the method of choice at European public health institutes.

## Computing an epidemic threshold with Farrington {#sec-farr-threshold}

The method runs in four steps, and each one has a figure to play with.

### Step 1: choose comparable weeks {#sec-farr-reference}

Counts rise and fall with the seasons, so this week is compared only with the
same time of year in past years. If this is week $x$ of year $y$, the
**baseline** is weeks $x-w$ to $x+w$ of the years $y-b$ to $y-1$: $b$ years
back, $w$ weeks either side. That gives

$$ n = b\,(2w+1) $$

baseline weeks. Farrington and colleagues used $b = 5$ and $w = 3$, so $n = 35$.

::: {#fig-farr-reference}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-farr-reference"></div>
```

The baseline for week 25 of 2026. Each row is one year of weekly counts, and the
teal bars are the baseline weeks. Change $b$ and $w$. The counts are simulated.
:::

This choice of weeks is how the method handles seasonality, so the model needs
no seasonal term. A wider window, or more years, gives more weeks to learn from.
But a wide window reaches into another part of the season, and old years may
reflect old reporting habits or laboratory methods [@farrington1996]. The
current year is never used, so an outbreak in progress cannot raise its own
baseline.

### Step 2: fit a line through the windows {#sec-farr-model}

Each baseline count $y_i$, in week $t_i$, has mean $\mu_i$ and variance
$\varphi\mu_i$. This is a quasi-Poisson model: a Poisson model in which the
variance may be larger than the mean. The only systematic effect is a
straight-line trend on the log scale:

$$ \log \mu_i = \alpha + \beta\, t_i. $$

Weeks are counted from the first baseline week, so the baseline weeks are
$t = 1$ to $7$, $53$ to $59$, and so on, and this week is $t_0 = 264$. The line
carried forward to $t_0$ gives the **expected count**,
$\hat\mu_0 = \exp(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta\, t_0)$. The scatter around the line
gives the **dispersion**, with Poisson scatter as the floor
(@sec-rki-dispersion):

$$ \hat\varphi = \max\left\{1,\ \frac{1}{n-p}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \omega_i\,
\frac{(y_i - \hat\mu_i)^2}{\hat\mu_i}\right\}, $$

where $p$ is 2 with the trend and 1 without. Every weight $\omega_i$ is 1 until
step 4.

::: {#fig-farr-fit}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-farr-fit"></div>
```

The 35 baseline weeks of @fig-farr-reference on the time axis, with the fitted
line carried forward to this week. Drag a year up or down: the line,
$\hat\varphi$ and the three trend checks update. The red dashed mark is the
threshold $U$ from step 3.
:::

The trend is kept only if all three checks pass [@farrington1996]:

1. the baseline spans at least 3 years;
2. $\beta$ is significant at the 5% level;
3. $\hat\mu_0$ is no larger than the largest baseline count.

The third check stops a steep line from running away when it is carried a year
past the data. If any check fails, the model is fitted again as a flat line.

### Step 3: set the threshold {#sec-farr-upper}

The threshold $U$ is the top of a prediction interval: the range this week's
count should fall in if nothing unusual is happening. It allows for the scatter
of the count ($\hat\varphi\hat\mu_0$) and for the uncertainty in $\hat\mu_0$.
It is built on the $2/3$ power scale, where counts are close to symmetric:

$$ U = \hat\mu_0\left(1 + \frac{2}{3}\, z\,
\sqrt{\frac{\hat\varphi\hat\mu_0 + \operatorname{Var}(\hat\mu_0)}{\hat\mu_0^{2}}}\,\right)^{3/2}. $$

By default `farrington()` uses $z = 1.96$, the top of a two-sided 95% interval
[@salmon2016]. The week raises an alarm when its count is above $U$, unless
fewer than 5 cases were reported in the last 4 weeks [@farrington1996].

### Step 4: discount old outbreaks {#sec-farr-reweight}

An old outbreak in the baseline pulls the line up and inflates $\hat\varphi$,
so the threshold rises and the next outbreak is harder to see. Farrington
therefore fits the model again, with less weight on weeks far above the line.
Each week gets a standardised residual $s_i$ (an Anscombe residual: its distance
from the line on the $2/3$ power scale, divided by its standard deviation), and

$$
\omega_i =
\begin{cases}
\gamma\, s_i^{-2}, & s_i > c,\\
\gamma, & s_i \le c,
\end{cases}
$$

where $\gamma$ makes the weights add up to $n$. Only weeks above the line can
lose weight. In the package, this refit comes straight after the first fit,
before the trend checks and the threshold.

::: {#fig-farr-reweight}
```{=html}
<div id="viz-farr-reweight"></div>
```

The baseline of @fig-farr-fit with an outbreak added to 2023. Hollow circles have
lost weight, and the paler the circle, the smaller its weight. The grey dashed
line is the fit with every week at full weight. Hover over or tap a circle to see
$s_i$ and its weight.
:::

The cut-off $c$ decides how much of the past is believed. For ordinary weeks
$s_i$ is roughly standard normal, so the 1996 cut-off $c = 1$ also shrinks about
1 ordinary week in 6. Those weeks carry the ordinary scatter, so $\hat\varphi$
and the threshold fall: choose *No outbreak* and *c = 1* to see it.
@noufaily2013 raised the cut-off to $c = 2.58$, which touches about 1 ordinary
week in 200. In a 35-week baseline, though, 2.58 can miss much of an old
outbreak: the outbreak inflates $\hat\varphi$, and a larger $\hat\varphi$
shrinks every residual, including its own. Noufaily and colleagues paired the
higher cut-off with a much longer baseline.

## The 2013 revision {#sec-farr-2013}

@noufaily2013 kept the four steps and changed the settings to reduce false
alarms.

| | 1996 | 2013 |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline weeks | 35 | 237 |
| Seasonality | the windows only | the windows, plus a 10-level seasonal factor for the weeks between them |
| Weeks just before this one | not used | used, except the last 26 |
| Trend | kept if all three checks pass | kept if checks 1 and 3 pass |
| Cut-off $c$ | 1 | 2.58 |
| Threshold | the formula in step 3 | a negative binomial quantile |

: The two versions of the method, with $b = 5$ and $w = 3$. {#tbl-farr-versions}

In a test on weekly counts of more than 2000 diseases, the false alarm rate fell
from 1.63% to below 0.9%. The share of outbreaks detected also fell, from 57% to
51% (negative binomial) and 53% (quasi-Poisson) [@enki2016]. Public Health
England replaced the original algorithm with the negative binomial version.

## Running it in R {#sec-farr-package}

Both versions are in R's `surveillance` package [@salmon2016].

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(surveillance)

# weekly: one row per week, with columns date (a Date) and cases
cases <- sts(observed = weekly$cases, epoch = weekly$date, frequency = 52)

res96 <- cases |> farrington(control = list(b = 5, w = 3, alpha = 0.05))

res13 <- cases |> farringtonFlexible(control = list(
  b = 5, w = 3,
  noPeriods = 10,               # 10-level seasonal factor
  pastWeeksNotIncluded = 26,
  pThresholdTrend = 1,          # no significance test for the trend
  weightsThreshold = 2.58,
  thresholdMethod = "nbPlugin",
  alpha = 0.05                  # one-sided in this function
))

autoplot(res13)                 # counts, threshold and alarms (ggplot2)
```

Two things catch people out:

- `alpha` is two-sided in `farrington()` but one-sided in
  `farringtonFlexible()`, so the same value gives a lower threshold, and more
  alarms, in the newer function.
- The defaults of `farringtonFlexible()` are neither version: the 1996 baseline,
  trend test and threshold, with the 2013 cut-off of 2.58. A misspelled name in
  `control` is ignored without a warning, so copy the names exactly.

## What an alarm means {#sec-farr-interpretation}

An alarm means this week's count is higher than the model predicted for this
time of year, at the chosen error rate. It is a prompt to check, not a confirmed
outbreak: at a one-sided 5% level, 100 series give about 5 chance alarms every
week. The design also has limits:

- It judges each week alone, so a slow, sustained rise can slip through.
  [CUSUM](cusum.qmd) adds up that evidence.
- It assumes the season comes at the same time every year. An early or late
  season is compared with the wrong weeks.
- It has no place for covariates (other drivers of the counts, such as
  rainfall). BODA adds them (@sec-bayes-threshold).
